title: What soil is made of
teaches: What is in a handful of soil, the three sizes of mineral grain, and how their mix decides what a bed is like to garden

blocks.text: Take a handful of soil from a bed that grows well, and another from the corner where nothing does. Squeeze them. One may crumble apart, gritty and loose; the other may stay in a sticky lump that keeps the print of your fingers. They look like the same brown stuff, and they are made of the same few things. What differs is how much of each, and how the pieces are put together.

About **half** of a good garden soil, by volume, is solid. Most of that is tiny broken pieces of rock, the [[minerals|mineral]], with a little [[organic matter|organic]] mixed through: the remains of plants and animals at every stage of rotting. The other half is not there at all. It is the gaps between the grains, the **pores**,[^porosity] and they are shared between [[water|water]] and [[air|air]].

blocks.caption: A handful of loam, by volume, a day after a good soaking

blocks.text: Roots need both halves of that empty space. They drink from the films of water on the grains and breathe from the air between them. A root sitting in pores full of water for days drowns; one in pores full of air dries out. Much of what this course is about, from digging to compost, comes back to keeping that space open and about half full.

The organic part is small, often only 2 to 6 parts in a hundred by weight, but it feeds the soil's life, glues grains into crumbs and holds water like a sponge; lessons 3 and 4 are about it. This lesson is about the minerals: rock that frost, rain, roots and lichens have been breaking into smaller pieces since long before there were gardens.[^slow-soil]

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Good soil is about half solid and half pore space.
The pores hold the [[water|water]] and the [[air|air]] that roots need: roughly half and half once a soaking has drained.

blocks.text: The mineral part comes in three sizes, sorted by how wide each grain is.[^size-limits] [[Sand|sand]] is anything from 2 mm down to 0.05 mm, big enough to see and to feel as grit. [[Silt|silt]] is smaller, down to 0.002 mm, too fine to see one by one: dry, it feels like flour. [[Clay|clay]] is smaller still, and its grains are flat plates,[^clay-plates] sticky when wet and hard as brick when dry. Anything bigger than 2 mm is gravel and stones, and doesn't count.

blocks.caption: The three sizes, blown up so that a clay plate is the size of a pea

blocks.text: Size matters because of surface. Take a sugar cube of rock and cut it in half, and in half again. The rock is no bigger, but every cut opens new faces. Keep cutting down to grains of [[clay|clay]] and the same cube has the surface of a rug.

blocks.caption: The surface of one cubic centimetre of rock, cut into smaller and smaller grains, with each square drawn to scale

blocks.text: Water clings to surfaces, and so do many plant nutrients. That one fact explains most of what gardeners say about soils. A [[clay|clay]] soil holds water and food because it has an enormous amount of surface to hold them on; a [[sand|sand]] soil lets both run straight through because it has so little. Clay plates are also so thin that real clays have far more surface than the cubes here: a teaspoon of some clays has the area of half a football pitch.[^surface-area]

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: [[Sand|sand]], [[silt|silt]] and [[clay|clay]] are three sizes of the same broken rock.
Smaller grains have more surface, and surface holds water and nutrients.

blocks.text: You can tell a lot about a soil with nothing but your hand and a little water. Sand feels gritty, silt silky, clay sticky, and the longer a ribbon of wet soil you can squeeze out between thumb and finger before it breaks, the more clay it holds. Soil surveyors do this in the field, and with practice they come within a few percent of a lab.

blocks.caption: Texture by feel: a few questions about a wet ball of soil

blocks.text: For a measurement, use a jar. The three sizes settle out of water at very different speeds: a sand grain sinks like a stone, while a clay plate can hang in the water for days.[^stokes]

blocks.caption: One jar of loam, shaken and set down: each size settles in its own time, and a pencil mark goes on the glass at the top of each

blocks.text: To try it, fill a straight-sided jar a third full of soil from the bed, with stones and roots picked out. Top it up with water to near the brim, add a teaspoon of dish soap to help the grains come apart, and shake it hard for a few minutes. Mark the side of the jar at the top of the [[sand|sand]] after a minute, at the top of the [[silt|silt]] after six hours, and at the top of the [[clay|clay]] when the water clears, a day or two later. Bits of [[organic matter|organic]] float, so skim them off. Each layer's height over the whole is its share of the mix, and the next part turns those heights into a name.

The mix of the three sizes is the soil's **texture**, and soil scientists name it from a triangle. Each corner is all of one size; a point inside is a mix. Twelve regions of the triangle each have a name, from sand to clay, and in the middle is **loam**: a mix in which none of the three takes over, roughly two parts [[sand|sand]], two of [[silt|silt]] and one of [[clay|clay]]. Set the three layers of a jar below and see where its soil lands.

blocks.caption: The soil texture triangle, read from the layers in a jar
blocks.task: Find the layers that make a loam

blocks.text: Look at how the regions are shaped, and try a few millimetres more clay in the jar. It takes 85 parts in a hundred of [[sand|sand]] for a soil to be called sand, but only 40 of [[clay|clay]] for it to be one of the clays, whatever the rest is. A little clay goes a long way, because its tiny plates fill the gaps between bigger grains and lend the whole soil their stickiness.

blocks.title: What texture means in the bed
points: **Sandy** soils drain fast and warm early in spring, but dry out quickly and let nutrients wash away.
**Loamy** soils hold water and nutrients and still let air in: what most vegetables want.
**Clayey** soils hold water and nutrients well, but drain slowly, pack hard and are slow to warm.

blocks.text: Texture is the one thing about a soil you can't change in a season. Turning a clay bed into a loam by digging in sand would take tonnes of it, and too little sand makes clay more like concrete, not less.[^sand-in-clay] What you *can* change is what lives among the grains and how they are stuck together: the next four lessons are about exactly that, and their answer works on sandy and clay soils alike.

blocks.title: Try it in the garden
points: Do the feel test on a pinch from each bed. Write down what you find.
Then set up a jar test from your main bed and read it over the next two days. Put its three layers into the triangle above, to see whether your hand got it right.

blocks.caption: Eight questions on what soil is made of

items.question: This bed dried out and cracked into plates like these. What is it rich in?
items.why: Clay plates shrink as they dry and swell when wet, so a clay soil cracks in a drought. Sand doesn't shrink at all.

items.question: In a jar test, which layer settles first?
items.why: The biggest grains sink fastest: sand is down in about a minute, silt over a few hours, and clay can take a day or two.

items.question: Rubbed between wet fingers, a pinch of soil feels gritty. What is it mostly?
items.why: Sand grains are big enough to feel one by one. Silt feels smooth and silky, clay sticky.

items.question: Roughly how much of a good garden soil, by volume, is pore space?
items.why: About half of a healthy soil is pores, shared between water and air. Pack it down and that share shrinks.

items.question: Why does a clay soil hold more water than a sandy one?
options: Its tiny grains have far more surface for water to cling to
Clay grains soak water up inside them like sponges
items.why: The same volume of rock in tiny plates has thousands of times the surface of sand grains, and water clings to surface.

items.question: A jar test gives 70% sand, 20% silt and 10% clay. What will the bed be like?
options: Quick to drain, and in need of watering more often
Slow to drain, and sticky after rain
items.why: That is a sandy loam. It drains and warms quickly, but holds less water and fewer nutrients than a loam.

items.question: Why do most vegetables do best in a loam?
options: It holds water and nutrients but still drains and lets air in
It is the richest in clay
It has no pore space to dry out
items.why: In a loam no one size takes over: the sand keeps it open, the clay holds water and nutrients, and the silt sits between.

items.question: Your clay bed drains slowly. What happens if you dig in a few bags of sand?
options: Very little, or it packs harder
It drains like a sandy soil
items.why: A few bags barely move the mix, and sand in clay can set hard. Organic matter, worked in or laid on top, is what opens up a clay soil.

learned: Soil is about half solid (minerals and a little organic matter) and half pores, shared by water and air.
Sand, silt and clay are the three sizes of mineral grain; the smaller the grain, the more surface it has to hold water and nutrients.
The feel test and the jar test measure the mix, and the texture triangle names it.
Texture can't be changed in a season, but what lives in the soil and how its grains stick together can.
next: Next: where water and air live, or why one bed floods after rain and another is dust by the weekend.

porosity.title: Porosity
porosity.text: The share of a soil's volume that is pores is its **porosity**. Most garden soils sit between 40 and 60 percent. Clay soils have more pore space than sandy ones, surprisingly, but in pores so small that water clings in them and drains slowly.

slow-soil.title: How long soil takes
slow-soil.text: Turning rock into a few centimetres of topsoil takes centuries; estimates run from about a hundred years to a thousand, depending on the rock and the climate. A bare bed can lose that much to one wet winter's rain. That is the real case for keeping soil covered, which lesson 7 comes back to.

size-limits.title: Where the limits fall
size-limits.text: These are the US Department of Agriculture's limits, used on most garden soil tests. The international system, used in much of Europe and Australia, puts the line between sand and silt at 0.02 mm instead of 0.05. Clay is under 0.002 mm in both.

clay-plates.title: What a clay plate is
clay-plates.text: Clay is more than finely ground rock. As minerals such as feldspar weather, they rebuild themselves into new ones, kaolinite, illite, smectite, made of sheets of silicon, aluminium and oxygen stacked like the pages of a book. Some of them, like smectite, let water in between the pages, which is why some clay soils swell when wet and crack open when they dry.

surface-area.title: Specific surface
surface-area.text: Soil scientists call surface per gram the **specific surface**. Sand has well under one square metre per gram. Kaolinite clay has 10 to 20, and smectite, whose sheets can be wetted on both faces, up to 800. A teaspoon of smectite, about 5 grams, has roughly 4,000 square metres of surface: more than half a football pitch.

stokes.title: Stokes' law
stokes.text: How fast a small grain sinks in still water goes with the *square* of its width, a rule George Stokes worked out in 1851. A grain ten times wider sinks a hundred times faster. That is why a minute separates the sand, but clay takes days.

sand-in-clay.title: Why sand can make clay worse
sand-in-clay.text: In a clay soil, a modest amount of sand doesn't touch grain to grain. The clay fills every gap around it, and the sand just adds solid where there were pores. Only when sand is most of the mix, well over half, do its grains rest on each other and leave open spaces. Builders mix sand and clay on purpose for exactly this reason: it makes adobe.
